The oldest traces of archaic humans in what is now France date from approximately 1.8 million years ago.[[16]](#cite_note-Jean_Carpentier_1987_p.17-26) [Neanderthals](/wiki/Neanderthal "Neanderthal") occupied the region into the [Upper Paleolithic](/wiki/Upper_Paleolithic "Upper Paleolithic") era but were slowly replaced by *[Homo sapiens](/wiki/Human "Human")* around 35,000 BC.[[17]](#cite_note-27) This period witnessed the emergence of [cave painting](/wiki/Cave_painting "Cave painting") in the [Dordogne](/wiki/Dordogne "Dordogne") and [Pyrenees](/wiki/Pyrenees "Pyrenees"), including at [Lascaux](/wiki/Lascaux "Lascaux"), dated to c. 18,000 BC.[[16]](#cite_note-Jean_Carpentier_1987_p.17-26) At the end of the [Last Glacial Period](/wiki/Last_Glacial_Period "Last Glacial Period") (10,000 BC), the climate became milder;[[16]](#cite_note-Jean_Carpentier_1987_p.17-26) from approximately 7,000 BC, this part of Western Europe entered the [Neolithic](/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic") era, and its inhabitants became [sedentary](/wiki/Sedentism "Sedentism").

After demographic and agricultural development between the 4th and 3rd millennia BC, [metallurgy appeared](/wiki/Three-age_system "Three-age system"), initially working gold, [copper](/wiki/Chalcolithic "Chalcolithic") and [bronze](/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age"), then later [iron](/wiki/Iron_Age "Iron Age").[[18]](#cite_note-28) France has numerous [megalithic](/wiki/Megalith "Megalith") sites from the Neolithic, including the [Carnac stones](/wiki/Carnac_stones "Carnac stones") site (approximately 3,300 BC).

Freiburg around 1900

The university had enough [endowments](/wiki/Financial_endowment "Financial endowment") and earnings to survive until the beginning of the regency of [Ludwig I, Grand Duke of Baden](/wiki/Ludwig_I,_Grand_Duke_of_Baden "Ludwig I, Grand Duke of Baden") in 1818. Finally in 1820, he saved the university with an annual contribution. Since then, the university has been named Albert Ludwigs University of Freiburg (*Albert-Ludwigs-Universität Freiburg*) as an acknowledgement of gratitude by the university and the citizens of Freiburg.

In the 1880s, the population of the student body and faculty started to grow quickly. The scientific reputation of Albert Ludwigs University attracted several researchers such as economist [Adolph Wagner](/wiki/Adolph_Wagner "Adolph Wagner"), historians [Georg von Below](/w/index.php?title=Georg_von_Below&action=edit&redlink=1 "Georg von Below (page does not exist)") and [Friedrich Meinecke](/wiki/Friedrich_Meinecke "Friedrich Meinecke"), and jurists [Karl von Amira](/wiki/Karl_von_Amira "Karl von Amira") and [Paul Lenel](/w/index.php?title=Paul_Lenel&action=edit&redlink=1 "Paul Lenel (page does not exist)").

In 1900, Freiburg became the first German university to accept female students. Before there had been no [women at German universities](/wiki/Women_at_German_universities "Women at German universities").

In the beginning of the 20th century, several new university buildings were built in the centre of Freiburg, such as the new main building in 1911. The university counted 3,000 students just before [World War I](/wiki/World_War_I "World War I").
